questions.q: Where does every ACL record in a ServiceNow instance actually live?
options: In a dedicated permissions engine separate from the database
On the sys_security_acl table
In the system properties list
Inside each individual business rule
questions.explain: Every access control rule, however it was created, is a record on sys_security_acl — there is no separate permission engine.

questions.q: Three ACLs apply to the same read attempt on a record. Two pass and one fails. What happens?
options: Access is denied, because every applicable ACL must pass
Access is granted, because a majority of the ACLs passed
Access is granted, because at least one ACL passed
The platform ignores the failing ACL since two already passed
questions.explain: ACL evaluation is an AND across all applicable ACLs — one failure is enough to deny the whole operation, regardless of how many others passed.

questions.q: A user has full read access to Incident but cannot create one. What does this tell you about how ACLs are organized?
options: Read and create are governed by completely separate ACL records for the same table
This is impossible, since one ACL always covers an entire table
The user's role was misconfigured and needs to be recreated
Create access is always granted automatically once read access is granted
questions.explain: ACLs are evaluated per operation — read, write, create, delete are each governed by their own ACL records, even on the same table.

questions.q: A user passes the table-level read ACL on Incident. Can a field-level ACL still deny them visibility into one specific field?
options: No, passing the table-level ACL guarantees access to every field
Yes, field-level ACLs are checked in addition to the table-level ACL, never instead of it
No, field-level ACLs only apply to write operations, never read
Yes, but only if the user has no roles assigned at all
questions.explain: Table-level access is necessary but not sufficient — any field-level ACL on a specific field still has to pass on top of it.

questions.q: Why does adding a new, narrower ACL to a table sometimes break access that previously worked?
options: New ACLs are evaluated before old ones and override them
It adds one more rule to the AND chain, and that new rule also has to pass now
ServiceNow automatically disables older ACLs when a new one is added
New ACLs only affect create and delete operations, never read or write
questions.explain: Since every applicable ACL must pass, adding a new one introduces an additional condition that access now has to satisfy too.
